data.Question: What is .NET Core? How is it different from .NET Framework?
data.Answer:
• Cross-platform (Windows, Linux, macOS)
  • Open source
  • Modular (NuGet-based)
  • High performance
  • Unified into .NET 5+ as a single platform

data.Question: What [ValidateNever] does?
data.Answer:
• [ValidateNever] is an attribute in ASP.NET Core that tells the model validation system to skip validation for a specific property
  • It's used when you want to exclude a property from model validation, even if it has validation attributes
  • Useful for properties that are set programmatically or come from sources other than user input
  • Prevents validation errors for properties that shouldn't be validated during model binding
  • Example: Use it on properties like IDs, timestamps, or computed values that are set by the application rather than user input

data.Question: What is the difference between .NET Framework and .NET Core / .NET?
data.Answer:
• Platform Support: .NET Framework is Windows-only, while .NET Core/.NET is cross-platform (Windows, Linux, macOS)
  • Open Source: .NET Framework is proprietary, .NET Core/.NET is open source
  • Deployment: .NET Framework requires system-wide installation, .NET Core/.NET supports self-contained deployments
  • Performance: .NET Core/.NET has better performance, lower memory usage, and faster startup times
  • Modularity: .NET Framework is monolithic, .NET Core/.NET is modular with NuGet packages
  • Versioning: .NET Framework uses version numbers (4.x), .NET Core/.NET uses unified versioning (.NET 5, 6, 7, 8+)
  • Development: .NET Framework is in maintenance mode, .NET Core/.NET is actively developed with new features
  • API Surface: .NET Core/.NET has a subset of .NET Framework APIs, with many modern alternatives

data.Question: Explain Dependency Injection in .NET Core
data.Answer:
• Definition: Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern that implements Inversion of Control (IoC) to manage dependencies between classes
  • Built-in Container: .NET Core includes a built-in DI container that's lightweight and easy to use
  • Registration: Services are registered in the Program.cs or Startup.cs using methods like AddSingleton, AddScoped, and AddTransient
  • Lifetime Types:
    • Singleton: One instance for the entire application lifetime
    • Scoped: One instance per HTTP request (in web apps)
    • Transient: New instance every time it's requested
  • Constructor Injection: Dependencies are injected through constructor parameters
  • Benefits: Loose coupling, testability, maintainability, and easier code management
  • Service Resolution: The DI container automatically resolves and injects dependencies when creating objects
  • Example: services.AddScoped<IUserService, UserService>(); registers a service that can be injected into controllers or other services

data.Question: Why should DbContext be Scoped and not Singleton?
data.Answer:
• Thread Safety: DbContext is not thread-safe. Using Singleton would cause multiple threads to access the same instance simultaneously, leading to race conditions and data corruption
  • State Management: DbContext maintains internal state (tracked entities, change tracker). A Singleton would accumulate state across all requests, causing memory leaks and incorrect behavior
  • Connection Management: Database connections should be short-lived. Singleton would keep connections open for the entire application lifetime, exhausting connection pools
  • Concurrency Issues: Multiple concurrent requests would share the same DbContext instance, causing conflicts when saving changes or querying data
  • Change Tracking: The change tracker would track entities from all requests, leading to unexpected behavior when calling SaveChanges()
  • Best Practice: Scoped lifetime ensures one DbContext per HTTP request, which is disposed after the request completes, maintaining proper isolation
  • Example: services.AddDbContext<ApplicationDbContext>(options => options.UseSqlServer(connectionString)); - This registers DbContext as Scoped by default

data.Question: How does middleware work in ASP.NET Core?
data.Answer:
• Definition: Middleware is software components that are assembled into an application pipeline to handle requests and responses
  • Request Pipeline: Middleware components are executed in the order they are registered, forming a request processing pipeline
  • Execution Flow: Each middleware can process the request before passing it to the next middleware, and process the response after the next middleware completes (like a chain)
  • Use Method: Middleware is registered using app.Use() or extension methods like app.UseAuthentication(), app.UseRouting(), etc.
  • Common Middleware:
    • Authentication/Authorization
    • Routing
    • Static Files
    • CORS
    • Exception Handling
    • Logging
  • Terminal Middleware: The last middleware in the pipeline (usually MVC/Razor Pages) handles the request and doesn't call next()
  • Short-Circuiting: Middleware can stop the pipeline by not calling next(), preventing subsequent middleware from executing
  • Example: app.Use(async (context, next) => { /* before */ await next(); /* after */ });

data.Question: How do you improve performance in ASP.NET Core?
data.Answer:
• Async/Await: Use asynchronous methods (async/await) to avoid blocking threads and improve scalability
  • Caching: Implement response caching, memory caching, or distributed caching to reduce database calls and improve response times
  • Database Optimization: Use compiled queries, avoid N+1 queries, use projections instead of loading full entities, and implement connection pooling
  • Response Compression: Enable response compression middleware to reduce payload size
  • Minimize Middleware: Remove unnecessary middleware and order middleware efficiently to reduce processing overhead
  • Use IMemoryCache/IDistributedCache: Cache frequently accessed data to avoid repeated computations or database queries
  • Pagination: Implement pagination for large datasets instead of loading all records
  • Compiled Models: Use compiled models in EF Core for better startup performance
  • Response Caching: Use [ResponseCache] attribute or response caching middleware for cacheable responses
  • Minimize Allocations: Use ArrayPool, StringBuilder, and avoid unnecessary object creation
  • Use ReadAsync/WriteAsync: For I/O operations, use async methods to prevent thread blocking

data.Question: What is N+1 problem and how do you solve it?
data.Answer:
• Definition: The N+1 problem occurs when you execute 1 query to fetch N records, and then execute N additional queries (one for each record) to fetch related data
  • Example: Loading 100 blogs (1 query) and then loading author for each blog (100 queries) = 101 total queries
  • Performance Impact: Causes excessive database round trips, leading to poor performance and increased latency
  • Solution 1 - Eager Loading: Use .Include() to load related data in a single query: context.Blogs.Include(b => b.Author).ToList()
  • Solution 2 - Explicit Loading: Use .Load() to explicitly load related data when needed: context.Entry(blog).Collection(b => b.Posts).Load()
  • Solution 3 - Projection: Use Select() to project only needed data, which automatically includes related entities: context.Blogs.Select(b => new { b.Title, b.Author.Name })
  • Solution 4 - Compiled Queries: Use compiled queries for repeated queries to improve performance
  • Solution 5 - Batch Loading: Load related data in batches using .ThenInclude() for nested relationships
  • Best Practice: Always use eager loading (.Include()) when you know you'll need related data, or use projections to fetch only required fields

data.Question: EF Core vs Dapper – when to use what?
data.Answer:
• EF Core - Use When:
    • You need rapid development and productivity
    • Working with complex object relationships and navigation properties
    • Need change tracking and automatic SQL generation
    • Want code-first migrations and database schema management
    • Building applications where developer productivity is prioritized
    • Need LINQ queries and type-safe database access
  • Dapper - Use When:
    • Performance is critical (micro-optimizations needed)
    • Working with existing stored procedures or complex SQL
    • Need full control over SQL queries
    • Building high-throughput applications (APIs, microservices)
    • Working with read-heavy applications
    • Team has strong SQL expertise
  • Performance: Dapper is faster (raw SQL, no overhead), EF Core has more overhead but is still performant
  • Learning Curve: EF Core is easier to learn, Dapper requires SQL knowledge
  • Maintenance: EF Core provides migrations and schema management, Dapper requires manual SQL script management
  • Hybrid Approach: Use EF Core for complex operations and Dapper for performance-critical queries

data.Question: How do you secure a .NET Core Web API?
data.Answer:
• Authentication: Implement authentication using JWT tokens, OAuth 2.0, or Identity Server. Use AddAuthentication() and AddJwtBearer() middleware
  • Authorization: Use [Authorize] attribute on controllers/actions, implement role-based (RBAC) or policy-based authorization
  • HTTPS: Always use HTTPS in production. Configure with app.UseHttpsRedirection() and enforce SSL/TLS
  • CORS: Configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing properly. Use AddCors() with specific origins, not wildcards in production
  • Input Validation: Use data annotations, FluentValidation, or model validation to validate all inputs and prevent injection attacks
  • SQL Injection Prevention: Use parameterized queries (EF Core does this automatically) or parameterized stored procedures
  • Rate Limiting: Implement rate limiting to prevent abuse and DDoS attacks using middleware or libraries like AspNetCoreRateLimit
  • API Keys: Use API keys for service-to-service authentication when appropriate
  • Secrets Management: Store sensitive data (connection strings, API keys) in Azure Key Vault, environment variables, or User Secrets (development)
  • Error Handling: Don't expose sensitive information in error messages. Use custom exception middleware
  • Logging & Monitoring: Implement security logging and monitoring to detect suspicious activities
  • Content Security: Validate content types, implement file upload restrictions, and sanitize user inputs

data.Question: How do .NET Core microservices communicate?
data.Answer:
• HTTP/REST APIs: Most common approach using HTTP/HTTPS with JSON. Services expose RESTful endpoints and communicate via HttpClient or IHttpClientFactory
  • gRPC: High-performance RPC framework using Protocol Buffers. Better for internal service-to-service communication. Use Grpc.Net.Client package
  • Message Queues: Asynchronous communication using message brokers like RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, or Apache Kafka. Use libraries like MassTransit or NServiceBus
  • Service Discovery: Services register and discover each other using tools like Consul, Eureka, or Kubernetes service discovery
  • API Gateway: Single entry point (Ocelot, YARP) that routes requests to appropriate microservices, handles authentication, and load balancing
  • Event-Driven Architecture: Services communicate via events using pub/sub patterns. Events can be published to message brokers or event stores
  • IHttpClientFactory: Recommended way to create HttpClient instances in .NET Core to avoid socket exhaustion and manage connections efficiently
  • Circuit Breaker Pattern: Use libraries like Polly to implement circuit breakers, retries, and resilience patterns
  • Service Mesh: Infrastructure layer (like Istio, Linkerd) that handles service-to-service communication, security, and observability
  • Direct Database Access: Avoid sharing databases between microservices. Each service should have its own database (Database per Service pattern)

data.Question: How do you handle configuration in different environments?
data.Answer:
• appsettings.json Files: Use appsettings.json for base configuration and appsettings.{Environment}.json (e.g., appsettings.Development.json, appsettings.Production.json) for environment-specific settings
  • Environment Variables: Set ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT to Development, Staging, or Production. Configuration is loaded in order: base file, then environment-specific file, then environment variables
  • Configuration Providers: Use IConfiguration interface to access configuration. Multiple providers can be chained: JSON files, environment variables, command-line arguments, user secrets
  • Options Pattern: Use IOptions<T>, IOptionsSnapshot<T>, or IOptionsMonitor<T> to bind configuration to strongly-typed classes
  • User Secrets: For development, use dotnet user-secrets to store sensitive data locally without committing to source control
  • Azure Key Vault: For production, integrate Azure Key Vault to store secrets securely using AddAzureKeyVault()
  • Configuration Priority: Later providers override earlier ones. Order: appsettings.json → appsettings.{Environment}.json → Environment Variables → Command Line
  • Strongly-Typed Configuration: Create configuration classes and bind them using services.Configure<MyOptions>(configuration.GetSection("MySection"))
  • Best Practice: Never commit sensitive data (passwords, API keys) to source control. Use environment variables, user secrets, or key vaults

data.Question: How do you handle logging and monitoring?
data.Answer:
• ILogger Interface: Use ILogger<T> or ILoggerFactory for logging. Inject via constructor: ILogger<MyService>
  • Log Levels: Use appropriate log levels: Trace, Debug, Information, Warning, Error, Critical
  • Structured Logging: Use structured logging with placeholders: logger.LogInformation("User {UserId} logged in", userId) instead of string concatenation
  • Logging Providers: Configure multiple providers: Console, Debug, EventSource, Application Insights, Serilog, NLog, or ELK Stack
  • Application Insights: Use Azure Application Insights for cloud applications. Add AddApplicationInsightsTelemetry() for automatic telemetry collection
  • Serilog: Popular third-party logging library with structured logging, multiple sinks (file, database, cloud), and better formatting
  • Health Checks: Implement health checks using AddHealthChecks() to monitor application and dependency health (database, external APIs)
  • Performance Monitoring: Track metrics like response times, request counts, error rates, and custom business metrics
  • Exception Logging: Use global exception middleware to log unhandled exceptions with full context and stack traces
  • Correlation IDs: Use correlation IDs to track requests across multiple services in microservices architecture
  • Log Filtering: Configure log filtering in appsettings.json to control log levels per namespace or category
  • Best Practice: Log at appropriate levels, include context, avoid logging sensitive data, and use structured logging for better querying

data.Question: How do you handle global exception handling?
data.Answer:
• Exception Middleware: Create custom exception handling middleware using app.UseExceptionHandler() or app.UseMiddleware<ExceptionHandlingMiddleware>() to catch all unhandled exceptions
  • Developer Exception Page: Use app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage() in development to see detailed error information. Never use in production
  • Custom Exception Middleware: Create a middleware class that catches exceptions, logs them, and returns appropriate error responses based on exception type
  • Exception Filters: Use IExceptionFilter or ExceptionFilterAttribute for MVC-specific exception handling at controller/action level
  • Problem Details: Return standardized error responses using RFC 7807 Problem Details format for consistent API error responses
  • Exception Types: Handle different exception types differently: ValidationException returns 400, NotFoundException returns 404, UnauthorizedException returns 401
  • Logging: Always log exceptions with full context (stack trace, request path, user info, correlation ID) before returning error response
  • Security: Don't expose sensitive information (stack traces, internal details) in production error responses. Return generic messages to clients
  • Error Response Model: Create a consistent error response model with properties like StatusCode, Message, Errors, and TraceId
  • Middleware Order: Place exception handling middleware early in the pipeline (before routing) to catch exceptions from all middleware
  • Example: app.UseExceptionHandler(errorApp => { errorApp.Run(async context => { /* handle exception */ }); });

data.Question: API is slow in production. How will you debug?
data.Answer:
• Application Insights/APM Tools: Use Application Insights, New Relic, or Datadog to identify slow endpoints, database queries, and external API calls with detailed timing information
  • Response Time Logging: Add middleware to log request/response times for each endpoint. Track slow requests (e.g., > 1 second)
  • Database Query Analysis: Enable EF Core query logging, use SQL Profiler, or Application Insights to identify slow queries, missing indexes, or N+1 problems
  • Performance Counters: Monitor CPU, memory, thread pool, and connection pool metrics to identify resource bottlenecks
  • Correlation IDs: Use correlation IDs to trace requests across services and identify which service is causing delays
  • Profiling Tools: Use dotTrace, PerfView, or Visual Studio Diagnostic Tools to profile CPU and memory usage in production
  • Check Dependencies: Monitor external API calls, database connections, cache hits/misses, and message queue processing times
  • Review Logs: Analyze structured logs for patterns: slow endpoints, frequent errors, high request volumes, or specific user scenarios
  • Load Testing: Reproduce the issue with load testing tools (JMeter, k6) to identify performance degradation under load
  • Code Review: Check for synchronous I/O operations, missing async/await, inefficient algorithms, or blocking calls
  • Network Analysis: Check network latency, DNS resolution times, and connection pool exhaustion
  • Common Issues: Look for missing indexes, inefficient queries, lack of caching, blocking async operations, memory leaks, or thread pool starvation

data.Question: Transient vs Scope vs singalton .net core?
data.Answer: Transient, Scoped, and Singleton define how long a service lives in the Dependency Injection (DI) container.

data.Question: How did you implement Rate Limiter?
data.Answer:
Rate Limiting in .NET 7+ is built-in via Microsoft.AspNetCore.RateLimiting middleware.

Step 1: Add Rate Limiting Services
builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(options =>
{
options.GlobalLimiter = PartitionedRateLimiter.Create<HttpContext, string>(context =>
RateLimitPartition.GetFixedWindowLimiter(
partitionKey: context.User.Identity?.Name ?? context.Request.Headers.Host.ToString(),
factory: _ => new FixedWindowRateLimiterOptions
{
AutoReplenishment = true,
PermitLimit = 100,
Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1)
}));
options.RejectionStatusCode = StatusCodes.Status429TooManyRequests;
});

Step 2: Use Middleware
app.UseRateLimiter();

Rate Limiter Algorithms:
  • Fixed Window: X requests per time window (e.g., 100 req/min)
  • Sliding Window: Smooths out burst traffic across segments
  • Token Bucket: Tokens replenish at fixed rate; allows bursts
  • Concurrency: Limits concurrent requests (not rate)

Named Policies:
options.AddFixedWindowLimiter("Api", opt => {
opt.PermitLimit = 10;
opt.Window = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10);
});

[EnableRateLimiting("Api")]
public class MyController : ControllerBase { }

Per-Client Limiting: Partition by IP, user ID, or API key using partitionKey.

For .NET 6 and earlier: Use AspNetCoreRateLimit NuGet package.
